title: Pilgrimage: Bodh Gaya
hookLine: the Mahabodhi temple and the bodhi tree, full of pilgrims from every school

cards: Before sunrise, the sound starts. A Tibetan monk on a cushion on the flagstones reads aloud from a long, loose-leaf text. A few steps away, a group in white chants in Pali.
Further on, Japanese pilgrims in a line strike a small hand drum. A woman from Thailand presses gold leaf onto a railing.

Above them rises a tall carved tower, and behind it a broad tree with heart-shaped leaves, its branches propped up and draped in cloth. They don't all practice alike. They have all walked to the same tree.
This is Bodh Gaya, and they remember it in plain words: here he woke up.

teach.h: A DELIGHTFUL GROVE BY A RIVER.
teach.b: Start with why he went there. In the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha looks back on his search. He had studied with teachers and left them, still unsatisfied.

Then he walked until he reached Uruvela, and found what he calls a delightful grove, with a clear river and a village nearby for alms: a good place, he says, for someone set on striving. So he sat down.
He didn't pick a holy place. He picked a good place, and it became holy because of what happened there. Next, the tree.
Bodhi means awakening; the tree is named for the night, not the other way around.

The opening of the monastic rule picks up just after: the Buddha sitting at the foot of the bodhi tree by the river, newly awakened, staying on in the joy of freedom. Today's tree isn't the same trunk.
Tradition says it comes down from the first through cuttings carried and replanted, and pilgrims treat it with that care. Then the temple.
The Mahabodhi temple rises beside the tree, and near it a stone seat marks where tradition says he sat.

And here's what a visitor carries home. At Bodh Gaya, Theravada, Tibetan, Zen, Pure Land and newer communities have built monasteries and practice side by side. This path has met the schools one at a time, chant by chant.
At the tree, they share one shade.

how: Pilgrims from many Buddhist schools come to Bodh Gaya in India to circle the Mahabodhi temple, sit or prostrate near the bodhi tree, chant, and offer flowers, lamps and robes.

o: a tour of temples to compare the schools
a vow to live by a sacred tree for life
a journey made to remember where he woke

p: the grove by a clear river

s: the Buddha chose Bodh Gaya because it was already a well-known holy site
in his own account he chose a delightful grove, a good place to strive. it became holy afterward.
pilgrims from many Buddhist schools practice side by side at Bodh Gaya
Theravada, Tibetan, Zen, Pure Land and newer communities build monasteries and practice there.
the tree at Bodh Gaya is named after the place
bodhi means awakening. the tree is named for what happened under it.

games.q: you've left your teachers, still searching. you reach a quiet grove with a clear river and a village nearby. what do you do?
o: keep walking to find a well-known holy place.
go back to your old teachers.
games.why: he sat down. in his own words, it was simply a good place for someone set on striving.

practice: Sit with your back straight and easy, and picture the tree: wide branches, leaves trembling, many chants at once. Sit beneath it in your mind; you don't need to wake up today, just sit where someone once did, and breathe.
When your thoughts wander, come back to the leaves.

wordCard.voice: Pilgrimage. A journey to remember. Its second great stop is Bodh Gaya, where the tree and the temple mark the Buddha's awakening. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit bodhi: awakening. the tree takes its name from it.

carryVoice: Your line: where he woke. Not a holy place to begin with, just a good one. Rest well.
